The data-manager warehouse

Raw & derived tables · SF1 reference · PIT universe · tear sheets & dead-stock exhibit

Author

data-manager project

Published

August 12, 2026

Abstract. ~/.prime/agent/data_manager.db is the single local SQLite source of point-in-time market data for the quant stack: 61.7M as-traded daily price rows (stocks and funds) back to 1998, a 3.15M-row SF1 fundamentals mirror in all six reporting dimensions, the full Sharadar securities master (31,742 instruments, survivorship-free), corporate actions (670k rows incl. delistings), and a locally derived point-in-time investable universe (universe_pit, 13.5M stock-days across 7,187 trading days). This report separates the raw Sharadar bulk tables from the locally derived ones, documents every SF1 column and reporting dimension, dissects the PIT universe (market-cap bins, sector and industry coverage), gives tear sheets for a mega / mid / small cap plus a dead-stock exhibit (Lehman Brothers), and reports freshness and data-quality findings. Numbers are as of the 2026-08-11 warehouse build; the PIT universe was rebuilt 2026-08-12 after a profile-carriage bug fix (see §6).

The dataset is split by lineage, not by name. The four raw families come from executable bulk zips (.csv.zip), always fetchable again; every derived table can be wiped and rebuilt with a single CLI command and no market-data requests.

The prices.adjustment contract. adjustment satisfies \(P^{\mathrm{adj}}_t = P^{\mathrm{as\text{-}traded}}_t \times \mathrm{adjustment}_t\) where \(P^{\mathrm{adj}}\) is the split- and dividend-adjusted close (Sharadar closeadj). The as-traded OHLC stored in the table is recovered from the bulk file by scaling the split-adjusted OHLC with the same-row split factor closeunadj/close; therefore close is the true as-traded price (it gaps at stock splits — see NVDA 2024-06-10 in §7) and the adjustment factor only matters for total-return series (§10 quantifies the no-trade and adjustment-tail rows).

3 Securities master & corporate actions

The two “who and what happened” tables. Both are raw Sharadar bulk files (tickers zip and actions zip), and both are survivorship-free — a name that delisted in 2008 keeps its row and its complete event history, which is exactly what the PIT universe and the dead-stock exhibit rely on.

3.1 The securities master (securities_master, 31,742 rows)

One row per instrument — US-listed stocks, ADRs, preferred, warrants, and funds — the vendor’s universe cube. The primary key is permaticker (the vendor’s stable internal id); ticker is the instrument’s current / last symbol. This matters: Lehman’s master row is LEHMQ, not LEH — the historical symbols live only in corporate_actions ticker-change rows, so never assume ticker was valid throughout the price history.

Semantics worth knowing. (1) date is the effective date — ex-date for dividends, split-date for splits — and it is the same date the price series moves on, so the rows pair 1:1 with the steps of the adjustment chain (§4). (2) value has no single unit: split ratio and $/share for dividends are clean and verified; spinoff value is shares per original share; tickerchangeto/from and relation put the counterparty in the contra columns; for delisted/acquisitionof rows, value is a vendor context number (delisting consideration in vendor units — not the last trade price, which lives in prices / master.lastpricedate), so verify before using it numerically. (3) Contra columns are N/A unless the event is paired. (4) The action ledger is not truncated per instrument: it is the complete hand-maintained vendor history, which is what makes it trustworthy evidence for delisting and bankruptcy questions (the LEHMQ exhibit in §8 is built straight off these rows).

4 Price coverage & depth

Daily as-traded OHLCV, survivorship-free (delisted names stay in the table). The stocks-vs-funds split uses the bulk-file origin (securities_master.table).

Stocks are continuous from 1997-01 (46,263,130 rows), funds from 1997-01 (15,475,363 rows). Stock coverage runs ~8,000–9,000 quoted tickers/year from 1998 onward (delisted names included, so yearly counts are quoted securities, not survivors); fund coverage grows from a few hundred to 6,434 tickers after 2010. The 8,391-row 1997 sliver is a bulk-file edge (pre-window rows for a handful of names), consistent with the Sharadar per-ticker window cap of ~28.6y noted at migration time.

4.1 The adjustment factor — what adjustment is, precisely

Every prices row carries adjustment, and the tear sheets plot “as-traded close” against “adjusted close (= close × adjustment)”. Behind that one multiplication sits the whole history of the stock’s corporate actions, collapsed into a single cumulative number per day.

Construction. adjustment(t) = closeadj(t) / close(t) where close is the as-traded close and closeadj is the vendor’s total-return-adjusted close (normalized so the factor is exactly 1.0 on the latest quote). The adjusted series is built one event at a time — each event multiplies every price before it by a factor:

event per-event factor applied to earlier prices
stock split s:1 (e.g. 4:1) 1/s (prices before the split shrink by 4×, so they stay comparable with post-split prices)
cash dividend d on the ex-date ≈ 1 − d/c with c the price level at the ex-date (the dividend is “reinvested” into the series)

Because the factors multiply, the chains telescope: the factor on a given day is just the product of the per-event factors of every event that happens after it — the same collapsed product for every day in an interval between two events. One number per day is therefore the whole chain, not a simplification:

adjustment(t)  =  Π  over events E with E.date > t   of  factor(E)      (up to vendor file precision)

Verified against the raw ledger. Rebuilding the chain from scratch — multiplying the measured per-event steps (split factors and dividend steps from corporate_actions, 1 − d/c from prices) backwards from the latest day, exactly reproduces the stored column: e.g. NVDA 2026-03-10 stored 0.9988039 vs reconstructed 0.9988027; NVDA 2021-07-19 stored 0.0249151 vs 0.0249120. The ~1e-4 relative gap on old rows is the vendor file’s own decimal rounding, not a semantic difference.

ticker event date stored step expected meaning
0 NVDA 4:1 split 2021-07-20 0.249998 1/4 adj. series −0.9% overnight (true return; raw was −75%)
1 NVDA 10:1 split 2024-06-10 0.100000 1/10 adj. series +0.7% (true return; raw was −90%)
2 NVDA 3:2 split 2007-09-11 0.666229 2/3 odd ratios handled the same way
3 AAPL 4:1 split 2020-08-31 0.250000 1/4 adj. series +3.4% overnight
4 AAPL 7:1 split 2014-06-09 0.142852 1/7 adj. series +1.6% overnight
5 C 1-for-10 reverse 2011-05-09 10.000000 10 reverse splits handled identically (factor > 1)
6 NVDA $0.25 dividend 2026-06-04 0.998859 1−d/c adj.-close return across the ex-date 218.66/(214.75·0.998859) = 1.0194 = (218.66+0.25)/214.75 — the dividend is inside the series

What the adjusted series is, and is not. adjusted(t2)/adjusted(t1) − 1 is the buy-and-hold total return from t1 to t2 with dividends reinvested (multiplicatively, at the ex-date price level) and splits “undone” — it is the number to use for returns work on past windows. It is not a tradable price history: on the latest day adjusted = as-traded by normalization, and going back it shrinks by every later split and dividend (NVDA’s 1999 adjusted close is $0.38 — nobody traded it at that price). Three honest caveats: (1) the dividend model is multiplicative (1 − d/c), so the factor depends on the price level at each ex-date — a convention, not literal reinvestment; (2) the factor embeds future events (it is normalized to the end of history) — exactly which uses that bites, and the one-line fix, are dissected in the next subsection; (3) a small share of rows carry junk factors (18,073 rows with the vendor’s 8.5e18 sentinel; ~1.4M rows with adjustment < 0.01 or > 100, mostly on zero-volume days) — filter adjustment BETWEEN 0.01 AND 100 when using it.

4.2 The look-ahead question — is adjustment safe for PIT backtests?

This is the subsection that matters most if you trade on this data. The “embeds future events” warning is precise in a way that admits an exact remedy — here is the whole argument, slowly, then the fix.

Step 1 — where the future lives. Restate the construction: adjustment(t) is the product of the factors of every corporate action after t, anchored so the latest quote has factor 1.0. So the factor on a 2021 date contains the 2024 split:

adjustment(NVDA, 2021-07-19) = 0.024915
   =  (dividend factors 2021→2026) × [10:1 split 2024] × [4:1 split 2021]

Nothing about that is wrong for returns — the chain is exactly what makes a long-horizon adjusted return equal the total return. But the level (literal adjusted price) at t was set partly by events that nobody knew on date t. A strategy deciding on date D may only use facts known by D; the stored level at t < D uses facts from after D. That is the look-ahead.

Step 2 — what actually cancels. Take the true as-of-D factor (events known by D only):

A(t; D) = product of factors of events E with  t < E ≤ D      (known by D)
adj(t)  = product of factors of events E with  E > t          (stored)

Both include the same events in (t, D]. They differ only in events after D — and that difference is one number for every t ≤ D:

adj(t) = A(t; D) × adj(D)                       ← the key identity

Because the chains telescope, the unknown tail Π_{E > D} factor(E) is exactly the factor stored at the as-of date itself. Consequently:

use of adjustment PIT-safe? remedy
daily / multi-day returns (adj(t2)/adj(t1) − 1) ✅ already safe — future factors cancel in the ratio; only events inside the window contribute none
momentum / ratio signals between two past dates ✅ same reason none
level of a total-return series as of decision date D ⚠️ scale includes events after D rebase: close(t) × adj(t) / adj(D)
absolute $ thresholds on an adjusted level (e.g. “adjusted price < $5”) ❌ never meaningful — the scale is total-return, not a price use as-traded close (as universe_pit does)
cross-stock comparison of adjusted levels ❌ levels are per-stock arbitrary scales compare returns, never levels

Step 3 — the fix is one division, not a rebuild. All the as-of-D information is already in the stored column. The point-in-time-correct total-return level at t, using only events known by D, is:

adjusted-PIT(t; D) = close(t) × adjustment(t) / adjustment(D)

At t = D this equals the as-traded close by construction; at t < D it folds in exactly the splits and dividends inside (t, D] and nothing after. The report’s accessor universe.adjusted_prices(..., asof=D) does this for you (and tests pin the behaviour; 88 green). If you read SQL directly, rebase with adjustment / (SELECT adjustment FROM prices WHERE ticker=? AND date<=? ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 1).

date as-traded stored adjusted level PIT level as of 2021-07-19
0 2020-12-03 535.84 13.34 535.54
1 2021-07-19 751.19 18.72 751.19

Read the second table left to right for NVDA with decision date 2021-07-19 (the 4:1 split happens that day, the 10:1 split is two years in the future): the stored adjusted level at 2020-12-03 ($13.34) is scaled by the 2024 split the strategy could not know; the PIT level (close × adj ÷ adj(D), $535.54) folds in only the events up to the decision date — and at the decision date itself the PIT level equals the as-traded price ($751.19), which is the correct, tradable, no- look-ahead anchor. The deviation table shows the identity holds to vendor precision (≤ ~3e-4 over a 5-year window).

Step 4 — what we actually do in the PIT backtests. Three rules, no exceptions:

  1. Membership, screens, thresholds — as-traded close, never adjusted. That is what universe_pit already does (as-traded close ≥ $2, as-traded $volume, quote ≤ 10 calendar days old, per-day “most recent valid quote” pointer — no post-hoc information anywhere in the membership).
  2. Signals and performance on returns — use adjusted-close ratios (adjusted_prices without asof, or close × adjustment yourself). They are PIT-correct by the cancellation in Step 2; no rebuild, no backfill, no special handling around splits and dividend ex-dates.
  3. Anywhere a total-return LEVEL is needed as of a decision date D (charts, TR indices, drawdown series, normalized relative strength) — rebase with adjustment(D): adjusted_prices(..., asof=D) or the one SQL division above. Never mix levels across different as-of dates, and never compare adjusted levels across stocks.

The old advice — “rebuild adjustments only from events known by date D” — is still true, but it is now exact and cheap: the rebuild is a division by the factor already stored at D. Nothing in the warehouse needs a new column or a maintenance job for this.

5 SF1 fundamentals: columns and reporting dimensions

The SF1 mirror is the fundamentals backbone. Every raw row carries 112 indicator fields; the table exposes 29 of them as typed columns (plus the six key fields) and keeps the full vendor row compressed in the data blob (zlib → JSON), so nothing is lost. Reporting dimensions are the key to using the mirror without look-ahead bias.

5.1 Reporting dimensions: As-Reported vs Most-Recent-Reported

Sharadar delivers fundamentals in six time dimensions — two views × three periods. The naming is AR = As-Reported, MR = Most-Recent (i.e. latest) Reported, with suffix Y annual, Q quarterly, T trailing twelve months (TTM):

dimension view period Sharadar definition (verbatim)
ARQ As-Reported quarterly “As Reported view (AR) excludes restatements, point-in-time view with data time-indexed to the date the form 10 regulatory filing was submitted to the SEC … may include multiple observations in a quarter if more than one filing is made during the quarter” — “typically suitable for back-testing”
ARY As-Reported annual same AR semantics, annual observations
ART As-Reported TTM same AR semantics, trailing-twelve-month observations
MRQ Most-Recent-Reported quarterly “Most Recent Reported view (MR) includes restatements, time indexed to the financial/report period … presents the most recently reported data for that reporting period” — “typically suitable for assessing business performance after restatements for mergers/divestitures”
MRY Most-Recent-Reported annual same MR semantics, annual observations
MRT Most-Recent-Reported TTM same MR semantics, TTM observations

Practical rules. Use AR* for point-in-time work (backtests, PIT screens) with the row’s date as the as-of availability date — date <= D is a valid point-in-time filter and is exactly what universe_pit does for shares. Use MR* for “what do we believe today” snapshots (build-ratios uses the latest MRY row). Restatements create AR-vs-MR splits on the same report period; when a company catches up after a reporting gap, ARQ may hold several filings for one quarter.

dimension rows first calendar date last calendar date

1 ART 660,802 1992-12-31 2026-06-30
2 ARY 173,633 1992-12-31 2026-12-31
3 MRQ 717,906 1990-06-30 2026-06-30
4 MRT 736,956 1990-06-30 2026-06-30

Row-level fields (all rows, all dimensions): ticker, dimension, date (Date Key — the as-of/publishable date; for AR rows 248 SEC filing date), calendardate (calendar date of the reporting period), reportperiod (fiscal period end), fiscalperiod (e.g. 2025-FY, 2025-Q3), lastupdated (vendor refresh timestamp), and the 112 indicators below.

5.2 Indicator dictionary: summary

There are 112 fields (7 key/date fields + 105 indicators; 29 typed in the sf1 table, the rest inside the compressed data blob) grouped into five statement families. The complete listing, every row shown, is in the appendix:

family indicators
0 Income statement 23
1 Balance sheet 33
2 Cash flow 14
3 Per-share & valuation 23
4 Margins & efficiency 12
5 total 112

What “in the blob” means. When the fundamentals zip was loaded we typed 29 frequently-used fields as real SQLite columns and stored the complete vendor row (all 105 indicator fields) as one compressed document in the data column (zlib → JSON). Plain SQL cannot see inside it: application code asks SQLite for the row(s) it needs, then decompresses one blob and reads whichever field it wants:

import json, zlib
blob = conn.execute(
    "SELECT data FROM sf1 WHERE ticker=? AND dimension=? AND reportperiod=?",
    ("AAPL", "ARY", "2025-09-30")).fetchone()[0]
row  = json.loads(zlib.decompress(blob).decode("utf-8"))
row["revenue"]   # any of the 105 indicator fields

So “queryable in the blob” means available in every row, at the cost of a decompress step — it is not a SQL filterable column. The 29 typed columns are the most-used fields (revenue, netinc, assets, equity, ncfo, capex, fcf, marketcap, ev, pe, pb, ps, eps, dps, divyield, roe, roa, roic, grossmargin, netmargin, ebitda, shareswa, shareswadil, currentratio, de, price, cashneq, liabilities), and the appendix marks each indicator’s location.

Notes on semantics (verified from vendor docs + live rows):

  • Scale. Every monetary field is raw as-reported units; the master’s scalemarketcap / scalerevenue columns are the Sharadar 10^scale convention but the bulk file’s SF1 rows are already unscaled (AAPL 1999 assets = 5.44B exactly).
  • FX. *usd fields are USD-normalized versions of the same line item (revenueusd, ebitusd, …); fxusd is the FX rate applied.
  • Shares. shareswa (weighted avg) and sharesbas (basic) are used for PIT market cap in universe_pit (price × shareswa, ARQ/ARY ≤ date).
  • Valuation blanks. pe1/ps1 are forward-looking (next-period); SF1 does not carry forward_pe or beta → those stay NULL in ratios (documented limitation).
  • TTM. ART/MRT rows exist (660k/737k) — TTM is a real dimension on the bulk file (the API serves 0 rows for it, another reason to use bulk).

6 PIT universe analysis

universe_pit is the locally derived investable universe — one row per (trading day, member) for 7,187 trading days (1998-01-14 → 2026-08-11). Algorithm (per ticker, no remote requests): walk its price rows keeping a rolling 20-session dollar-volume window and a pointer to the latest as-reported shares (SF1 ARQ/ARY date ≤ row date); a price row is valid when as-traded close ≥ $2, rolling avg $volume ≥ $5M with ≥ 10 sessions, and PIT mcap = close × shares ≥ $300M. Valid rows merge into runs that extend at most max_quote_age = 10 calendar days past the last fresh quote, then expand onto the global trading calendar.

2026-08-12 fix (important). The original build stored the run-start quote’s price/mcap/dvol for the whole run — a continuously trading name has one run from 1998 to today, so AAPL carried $19.75 (1998) as its 2026 profile. Membership dates were correct; the attached profile was not. Rebuilt so each member day carries the most recent valid quote ≤ that day (regression-tested; tests/test_db.py). All PIT numbers in this section use the rebuilt table.

Membership grows from 776 names (1998-01-14) to 2,435 (2026-08-11); the 2020 crash bottom holds 2,093 members (2020-03-23). The chart’s plateau-and-step shape reflects listing standards (more names pass the $5M-dollar-volume screen over time) rather than definition changes; the full range is re-runnable via build-universe-pit --history with different thresholds.

11 Accessing the data (SQL & accessor API)

Two layers, both documented end-to-end in the repo’s AGENTS.md (the canonical guide for downstream consumers — this section is the short form).

11.1 The accessor functions (in this repo)

function (module) returns
db.connect() (data_manager.db) a WAL-mode SQLite connection (tuned pragmas, schema ensured) — the normal entry for in-repo jobs
universe.adjusted_prices(ticker, start=None, end=None) per-day dicts date/open/high/low/close/volume/adjustment plus adjusted_open/.../adjusted_close (= raw × adjustment); volume left as traded
universe._hydrate_sf1(conn, ticker, dimension) decompressed full SF1 rows (all 105 fields) as dicts
universe.master_stocks(conn, isdelisted=None) all stock tickers (table='stocks'; honors DM_SHARD/DM_SHARDS)
universe.universe_tickers(conn) / etfs.etf_tickers() universe / ETF manifest ticker lists
CLI data-manager status live coverage snapshot

There is no ORM: everything else is plain SQL over one of the connection entry points.

11.2 Plain SQL (read-only)

Outside this repo, prefer the read-only URI so nothing can ever be written:

import sqlite3, pathlib
conn = sqlite3.connect(
    f"file:{pathlib.Path.home()}/.prime/agent/data_manager.db?mode=ro",
    uri=True)
conn.execute("PRAGMA cache_size=-65536"); conn.execute("PRAGMA mmap_size=134217728")
task SQL
daily bars / total returns SELECT date, close, volume, adjustment FROM prices WHERE ticker=? [AND date>=?] and compute close*adjustment yourself; or adjusted_prices
cross-section on date D SELECT * FROM prices WHERE date=? (uses idx_prices_date)
PIT shares / mcap SELECT shareswa FROM sf1 WHERE ticker=? AND dimension IN ('ARQ','ARY') AND date<=? ORDER BY date DESC LIMIT 1
investable members on D SELECT * FROM universe_pit WHERE as_of=? (uses idx_pit_asof)
fundamentals history SELECT * FROM sf1 WHERE ticker=? AND dimension='ARY' ORDER BY reportperiod (+ data blob for untyped fields)
delisting evidence corporate_actions rows with action IN ('delisted','bankruptcyliquidation')

11.3 Gotchas (condensed)

  1. close is as-traded and gaps at splits; use close*adjustment only for total-return series; screen volume=0 and adjustment outliers (0a79). 2. SF1 has six dimensions: AR* = as-reported (PIT-safe via date<=D), MR* = most-recent (restatements included). 3. Master PK is permaticker; ticker is the last/current symbol. 4. GICS classifications cover only the 2,589 iShares-era names. 5. ratios.forward_pe and beta are NULL by construction. 6. Never write to the DB from a consumer; WAL supports concurrent readers.

12 Database hygiene

The warehouse is refreshed by two commands, then verified:

  1. uv run data-manager status — baseline row counts and the snapshots pull ledger.
  2. uv run data-manager bulk-update — compares each table’s bulk zip against the server’s modified stamp (manifest in ~/.prime/agent/bulk/_manifest.json), re-downloads only changed files, reloads those tables with INSERT OR REPLACE (prices full reload ≈ 12 min), re-derives piotroski / quarterly / ratios, and rebuilds universe_pit --history (≈ 12 min, 13.5M rows). Logs in logs/.
  3. uv run data-manager optimize-db --backup <path> — consistent backup, WAL checkpoint, ANALYZE, quick_check, VACUUM (≈ 3 min; DB ≈ 16 GB). Run after every update; keep one backup per full rebuild.

Cadence. The Sharadar bulk zips refresh daily; a morning bulk-update + optimize-db keeps the warehouse current (worst case a few hundred MB–2 GB of downloads). bulk-fromzero is the full wipe-and-rebuild path (e.g., after a provider or schema change).
